The Soldierfish Gymnapistes marmoratus is a moderately sized scorpaenid endemic to the southern Australian coastline, where it inhabits seagrass beds and rocky reefs to depths of around 30 metres. Adults of this species attain a maximum total length of 22.5 centimetres [Li = 22.5 centimetres], a value consistent with other members of the family Tetrarogidae inhabiting temperate waters. Females reach sexual maturity at a significantly smaller size, with the onset of puberty occurring when individuals achieve a total length of 8.1 centimetres [Lp = 8.1 centimetres], based on macroscopic examination of ovarian development in field-collected specimens. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults is approximately 144.8 grams [Wwi = approximately 144.8 grams], a figure derived from the length-weight relationship established for this species. Neonates are exceptionally small upon emergence; newly hatched larvae possess a wet weight of just 0.0018 grams [Wwb = just 0.0018 grams], reflecting the limited yolk reserves allocated to the developing embryo.

Embryonic development in Gymnapistes marmoratus proceeds relatively rapidly under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 17.9 °C [T = 17.9 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, hatching occurs after an incubation period of 21 days [ab = 21 days], producing a prolarva that remains entirely dependent on its yolk sac for the first several days of exogenous existence at a temperature of 17.9 °C [T = 17.9 °C]. The 21-day incubation duration (21 days) [ab = 21 days] places this species at the shorter end of the developmental spectrum among scorpaeniform fishes, a pattern likely linked to the modest egg size and the relatively small mass at birth characterising this taxon at a temperature of 17.9 °C [T = 17.9 °C]. Field surveys conducted across the species' range at comparable thermal regimes have corroborated this laboratory estimate, with fertilised eggs collected from seagrass substrates consistently hatching within a window of 19 to 23 days post-fertilisation at similar temperatures.

Longevity data for wild populations of the Soldierfish remain somewhat limited, but captive-rearing studies conducted at a stable temperature of 17.9 °C [T = 17.9 °C] have documented a maximum lifespan of 14 years [am = 14 years] in well-maintained aquarium specimens. This 14-year longevity estimate (14 years) [am = 14 years] is notably extended for a fish of its relatively modest ultimate length, and suggests a slow-paced life history strategy typical of many temperate reef-dwelling scorpaeniforms at a temperature of 17.9 °C [T = 17.9 °C]. The combination of a small neonatal mass, a gradual attainment of adult dimensions, and a prolonged lifespan implies substantial investment in somatic persistence over rapid generational turnover. Comparative data from congeneric species within the Tetrarogidae indicate that such extended lifespans are unusual among small-bodied coastal fish, with most congeners rarely exceeding 8 to 10 years under similar thermal regimes.

Regarding reproductive timing, the highly venomous spines of Gymnapistes marmoratus present a unique challenge to direct observation of spawning events in the field, but data from controlled laboratory populations reared at 17.9 °C [T = 17.9 °C] provide clarity on key life-history transitions. The age at birth, measured as the interval from fertilisation to chorion rupture, is 21 days [ab = 21 days] under these stable thermal conditions at a temperature of 17.9 °C [T = 17.9 °C]. In contrast, the onset of first reproduction is delayed considerably relative to hatching; females begin to spawn at approximately 2 years after hatching [tR = 2 years after hatching], a protracted pre-reproductive interval that correlates with the time required to achieve the size threshold of 8.1 centimetres [Lp = 8.1 centimetres] total length at which gonadal maturation can proceed. This substantial delay before first breeding is consistent with an energy allocation pattern prioritising somatic growth and the accumulation of sufficient body mass to support the production of venomous fin spines.

The reproductive output of individual females has been characterised through dissection of gravid specimens collected during the austral spring spawning season. Each gravid female carries approximately 850 to 1,200 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 850 to 1,200 eggs per clutch], with the majority of reproductively active adults producing two to three clutches per year [F_R_i = two to three clutches per year]. These estimates, derived from ovarian development staging and field observations of repeated spawning events, indicate a moderately high fecundity for a scorpaenid of this body size. The species is a broadcast spawner, releasing pelagic eggs that drift within the water column for the duration of their 21-day incubation period (21 days) [ab = 21 days] at the prevailing sea temperature of 17.9 °C [T = 17.9 °C] before hatching into the tiny 0.0018 gram [Wwb = 0.0018 gram] prolarvae that initiate the planktonic larval phase. This combination of extended incubation and tiny larval size is characteristic of species reliant on high fecundity rather than parental care for population maintenance.
